Add sources with `--json` to capture IDs:\\r\\n   ```bash\\r\\n   notebooklm source add \\"https://url1.com\\" --json  # → {\\"source_id\\": \\"abc...\\"}\\r\\n   notebooklm source add \\"https://url2.com\\" --json  # → {\\"source_id\\": \\"def...\\"}\\r\\n   ```\\r\\n2. **Spawn a background agent** to wait for all sources:\\r\\n   ```\\r\\n   Task(\\r\\n     prompt=\\"Wait for sources {source_ids} in notebook {notebook_id} to be ready.\\r\\n             For each: notebooklm source wait {id} -n {notebook_id} --timeout 120\\r\\n             Report when all ready or if any fail.\\",\\r\\n     subagent_type=\\"general-purpose\\"\\r\\n   )\\r\\n   ```\\r\\n3. Main conversation continues while agent waits\\r\\n4. Once sources are ready, proceed with chat or generation\\r\\n\\r\\n**Why wait for sources?** Sources must be indexed before chat or generation. Takes 10-60 seconds per source.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Deep Web Research (Subagent Pattern)\\r\\n**Time:** 2-5 minutes, runs in background\\r\\n\\r\\nDeep research finds and analyzes web sources on a topic:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Create notebook: `notebooklm create \\"Research: [topic]\\"`\\r\\n2. Start deep research (non-blocking):\\r\\n   ```bash\\r\\n   notebooklm source add-research \\"topic query\\" --mode deep --no-wait\\r\\n   ```\\r\\n3. **Spawn a background agent** to wait and import:\\r\\n   ```\\r\\n   Task(\\r\\n     prompt=\\"Wait for research in notebook {notebook_id} to complete and import sources.\\r\\n             Use: notebooklm research wait -n {notebook_id} --import-all --timeout 300\\r\\n             Report how many sources were imported.\\",\\r\\n     subagent_type=\\"general-purpose\\"\\r\\n   )\\r\\n   ```\\r\\n4. Main conversation continues while agent waits\\r\\n5. When agent completes, sources are imported automatically\\r\\n\\r\\n**Alternative (blocking):** For simple cases, omit `--no-wait`:\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nnotebooklm source add-research \\"topic\\" --mode deep --import-all\\r\\n# Blocks for up to 5 minutes\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**When to use each mode:**\\r\\n- `--mode fast`: Specific topic, quick overview needed (5-10 sources, seconds)\\r\\n- `--mode deep`: Broad topic, comprehensive analysis needed (20+ sources, 2-5 min)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Research sources:**\\r\\n- `--from web`: Search the web (default)\\r\\n- `--from drive`: Search Google Drive\\r\\n\\r\\n## Output Style\\r\\n\\r\\n**Progress updates:** Brief status for each step\\r\\n- \\"Creating notebook \'Research: AI\'...\\"\\r\\n- \\"Adding source: https://example.com...\\"\\r\\n- \\"Starting audio generation... (task ID: abc123)\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Fire-and-forget for long operations:**\\r\\n- Start generation, return artifact ID immediately\\r\\n- Do NOT poll or wait in main conversation - generation takes 5-45 minutes (see timing table)\\r\\n- User checks status manually, OR use subagent with `artifact wait`\\r\\n\\r\\n**JSON output:** Use `--json` flag for machine-readable output:\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nnotebooklm list --json\\r\\nnotebooklm auth check --json\\r\\nnotebooklm source list --json\\r\\nnotebooklm artifact list --json\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**JSON schemas (key fields):**\\r\\n\\r\\n`notebooklm list --json`:\\r\\n```json\\r\\n{\\"notebooks\\": [{\\"id\\": \\"...\\", \\"title\\": \\"...\\", \\"created_at\\": \\"...\\"}]}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n`notebooklm auth check --json`:\\r\\n```json\\r\\n{\\"checks\\": {\\"storage_exists\\": true, \\"json_valid\\": true, \\"cookies_present\\": true, \\"sid_cookie\\": true, \\"token_fetch\\": true}, \\"details\\": {\\"storage_path\\": \\"...\\", \\"auth_source\\": \\"file\\", \\"cookies_found\\": [\\"SID\\", \\"HSID\\", \\"...\\"], \\"cookie_domains\\": [\\".google.com\\"]}}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n`notebooklm source list --json`:\\r\\n```json\\r\\n{\\"sources\\": [{\\"id\\": \\"...\\", \\"title\\": \\"...\\", \\"status\\": \\"ready|processing|error\\"}]}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n`notebooklm artifact list --json`:\\r\\n```json\\r\\n{\\"artifacts\\": [{\\"id\\": \\"...\\", \\"title\\": \\"...\\", \\"type\\": \\"Audio Overview\\", \\"status\\": \\"in_progress|pending|completed|unknown\\"}]}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Status values:**\\r\\n- Sources: `processing` → `ready` (or `error`)\\r\\n- Artifacts: `pending` or `in_progress` → `completed` (or `unknown`)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Error Handling\\r\\n\\r\\n**On failure, offer the user a choice:**\\r\\n1. Retry the operation\\r\\n2. Skip and continue with something else\\r\\n3. Investigate the error\\r\\n\\r\\n**Error decision tree:**\\r\\n\\r\\n| Error | Cause | Action |\\r\\n|-------|-------|--------|\\r\\n| Auth/cookie error | Session expired | Run `notebooklm auth check` then `notebooklm login` |\\r\\n| \\"No notebook context\\" | Context not set | Use `-n <id>` or `--notebook <id>` flag (parallel), or `notebooklm use <id>` (single-agent) |\\r\\n| \\"No result found for RPC ID\\" | Rate limiting | Wait 5-10 min, retry |\\r\\n| `GENERATION_FAILED` | Google rate limit | Wait and retry later |\\r\\n| Download fails | Generation incomplete | Check `artifact list` for status |\\r\\n| Invalid notebook/source ID | Wrong ID | Run `notebooklm list` to verify |\\r\\n| RPC protocol error | Google changed APIs | May need CLI update |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Exit Codes\\r\\n\\r\\nAll commands use consistent exit codes:\\r\\n\\r\\n| Code | Meaning | Action |\\r\\n|------|---------|--------|\\r\\n| 0 | Success | Continue |\\r\\n| 1 | Error (not found, processing failed) | Check stderr, see Error Handling |\\r\\n| 2 | Timeout (wait commands only) | Extend timeout or check status manually |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Examples:**\\r\\n- `source wait` returns 1 if source not found or processing failed\\r\\n- `artifact wait` returns 2 if timeout reached before completion\\r\\n- `generate` returns 1 if rate limited (check stderr for details)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Known Limitations\\r\\n\\r\\n**Rate limiting:** Audio, video, quiz, flashcards, infographic, and slide deck generation may fail due to Google\'s rate limits. This is an API limitation, not a bug.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Reliable operations:** These always work:\\r\\n- Notebooks (list, create, delete, rename)\\r\\n- Sources (add, list, delete)\\r\\n- Chat/queries\\r\\n- Mind-map, study-guide, report, data-table generation\\r\\n\\r\\n**Unreliable operations:** These may fail with rate limiting:\\r\\n- Audio (podcast) generation\\r\\n- Video generation\\r\\n- Quiz and flashcard generation\\r\\n- Infographic and slide deck generation\\r\\n\\r\\n**Workaround:** If generation fails:\\r\\n1. Check status: `notebooklm artifact list`\\r\\n2. Retry after 5-10 minutes\\r\\n3. Use the NotebookLM web UI as fallback\\r\\n\\r\\n**Processing times vary significantly.** Use the subagent pattern for long operations:\\r\\n\\r\\n| Operation | Typical time | Suggested timeout |\\r\\n|-----------|--------------|-------------------|\\r\\n| Source processing | 30s - 10 min | 600s |\\r\\n| Research (fast) | 30s - 2 min | 180s |\\r\\n| Research (deep) | 15 - 30+ min | 1800s |\\r\\n| Notes | instant | n/a |\\r\\n| Mind-map | instant (sync) | n/a |\\r\\n| Quiz, flashcards | 5 - 15 min | 900s |\\r\\n| Report, data-table | 5 - 15 min | 900s |\\r\\n| Audio generation | 10 - 20 min | 1200s |\\r\\n| Video generation | 15 - 45 min | 2700s |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Polling intervals:** When checking status manually, poll every 15-30 seconds to avoid excessive API calls.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Language Configuration\\r\\n\\r\\nLanguage setting controls the output language for generated artifacts (audio, video, etc.).\\r\\n\\r\\n**Important:** Language is a **GLOBAL** setting that affects all notebooks in your account.\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\n# List all 80+ supported languages with native names\\r\\nnotebooklm language list\\r\\n\\r\\n# Show current language setting\\r\\nnotebooklm language get\\r\\n\\r\\n# Set language for artifact generation\\r\\nnotebooklm language set zh_Hans  # Simplified Chinese\\r\\nnotebooklm language set ja       # Japanese\\r\\nnotebooklm language set en       # English (default)\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Common language codes:**\\r\\n| Code | Language |\\r\\n|------|----------|\\r\\n| `en` | English |\\r\\n| `zh_Hans` | 中文（简体） - Simplified Chinese |\\r\\n| `zh_Hant` | 中文（繁體） - Traditional Chinese |\\r\\n| `ja` | 日本語 - Japanese |\\r\\n| `ko` | 한국어 - Korean |\\r\\n| `es` | Español - Spanish |\\r\\n| `fr` | Français - French |\\r\\n| `de` | Deutsch - German |\\r\\n| `pt_BR` | Português (Brasil) |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Override per command:** Use `--language` flag on generate commands:\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nnotebooklm generate audio --language ja   # Japanese podcast\\r\\nnotebooklm generate video --language zh_Hans  # Chinese video\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Offline mode:** Use `--local` flag to skip server sync:\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nnotebooklm language set zh_Hans --local  # Save locally only\\r\\nnotebooklm language get --local  # Read local config only\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## Troubleshooting\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nnotebooklm --help              # Main commands\\r\\nnotebooklm auth check          # Diagnose auth issues\\r\\nnotebooklm auth check --test   # Full auth validation with network test\\r\\nnotebooklm notebook --help     # Notebook management\\r\\nnotebooklm source --help       # Source management\\r\\nnotebooklm research --help     # Research status/wait\\r\\nnotebooklm generate --help     # Content generation\\r\\nnotebooklm artifact --help     # Artifact management\\r\\nnotebooklm download --help     # Download content\\r\\nnotebooklm language --help     # Language settings\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Diagnose auth:** `notebooklm auth check` - shows cookie domains, storage path, validation status\\r\\n**Re-authenticate:** `notebooklm login`\\r\\n**Check version:** `notebooklm --version`\\r\\n**Refresh a CLI-managed install:** `notebooklm skill install`\\r\\n"}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 4.2 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"f35c33","wall_time_seconds":0.3608519,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":4010,"output":"# Conditional Logic: What the Rule Gives You\\r\\n\\r\\nDraft for Joshua\'s review · 2026-10-02\\r\\n\\r\\nThese six lessons form the opening chapter. Each teaches one idea, works through an example, and gives the student a small task before the attached practice. Visual and drill directions for our review are at the end, separate from the student copy. All new practice examples below are original draft examples.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 1. Start with a guarantee\\r\\n\\r\\nTake this statement:\\r\\n\\r\\n> All dogs are mammals.\\r\\n\\r\\nNow suppose I tell you that Luna is a dog. You know something else about Luna: she\'s a mammal.\\r\\n\\r\\nYou didn\'t need another fact about her. The rule already covers every dog, and Luna falls inside that group.\\r\\n\\r\\nWe can say the same rule another way:\\r\\n\\r\\n> If something is a dog, then it is a mammal.\\r\\n\\r\\nThat\'s a conditional. It tells you that **when one condition is met, another must be met too.**\\r\\n\\r\\nNotice the guarantee. The statement doesn\'t say dogs are usually mammals. It leaves no room for a dog that isn\'t a mammal.\\r\\n\\r\\nWe can write the relationship like this:\\r\\n\\r\\n**Dog → Mammal**\\r\\n\\r\\nRead the arrow as “if this is true, then that must be true.”\\r\\n\\r\\nThe rule doesn\'t tell us that a particular dog exists. It tells us what must be true of anything that is a dog. When we add the fact about Luna, we can apply the rule to her.\\r\\n\\r\\n### See the relationship\\r\\n\\r\\nImagine a box containing every mammal. Every dog has to fit inside that box. Mammals can sit outside the dog box, but dogs can\'t sit outside the mammal box.\\r\\n\\r\\nThat\'s why knowing “dog” gives us “mammal.”\\r\\n\\r\\n### Your turn\\r\\n\\r\\n> All volunteers wear badges. Ari is a volunteer.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhat does the rule guarantee about Ari?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details>\\r\\n<summary>See the reasoning</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nAri wears a badge. The rule covers every volunteer, and Ari is a volunteer. **Volunteer → Wears a badge.**\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep this:** A conditional tells you what must follow when its condition is met.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 2. Why the direction matters\\r\\n\\r\\nLet\'s stay with the same rule:\\r\\n\\r\\n**Dog → Mammal**\\r\\n\\r\\nIf I tell you Luna is a dog, you know she\'s a mammal.\\r\\n\\r\\nBut if I tell you Luna is a mammal, do you know she\'s a dog? No. She could be a cat. The rule has room for mammals that aren\'t dogs.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe arrow gives us a direction. Switching that direction changes the claim.\\r\\n\\r\\nThat\'s a major part of conditional reasoning on the LSAT. You need to know what a rule gives you, and where someone has gone beyond it.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn a Must Be True question, you may apply a rule to a fact. In a Flaw question, someone may reverse the rule and claim more than the premises establish. In a Sufficient Assumption question, you may need a missing rule that connects the evidence to the conclusion.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe question changes. The relationship still matters.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Compare the two moves\\r\\n\\r\\n| What we know | What we can conclude | Why |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| Luna is a dog. | Luna is a mammal. | The rule covers every dog. |\\r\\n| Luna is a mammal. | We don\'t know whether Luna is a dog. | Other mammals are allowed. |\\r\\n\\r\\n### Your turn\\r\\n\\r\\n> Every volunteer wears a badge. Ari wears a badge.\\r\\n\\r\\nDoes that establish that Ari is a volunteer? Explain your answer using the rule.\\r\\n\\r\\n<details>\\r\\n<summary>See the reasoning</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nNo. The rule requires volunteers to wear badges. It doesn\'t say that only volunteers wear them. Ari could be a staff member who also wears a badge.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep this:** Follow the direction the rule gives you. Before accepting a conclusion, check that the rule actually reaches it.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 3. Sufficient means enough\\r\\n\\r\\nWe have names for the two sides of a conditional. Start with the left:\\r\\n\\r\\n**Dog → Mammal**\\r\\n\\r\\nBeing a dog is **sufficient** for being a mammal. It\'s enough. Once we know something is a dog, we have what we need to conclude that it\'s a mammal.\\r\\n\\r\\nYou can think of the sufficient condition as the trigger. When it is met, the rule gives you the other side.\\r\\n\\r\\n> If a student earns full credit, that student passes the assignment.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Earns full credit → Passes**\\r\\n\\r\\nEarning full credit is sufficient for passing. Suppose Maya earned full credit. Put yourself in her situation: under this rule, what do you know? She passes.\\r\\n\\r\\nBut full credit might not be the only way to pass. A student could earn less than full credit and still pass. “Enough” doesn\'t mean “the only way.”\\r\\n\\r\\n### Your turn\\r\\n\\r\\n> If a person wins the race, that person receives a medal.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhich condition is enough to guarantee the other? Then write the arrow.\\r\\n\\r\\n<details>\\r\\n<summary>See the reasoning</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nWinning is enough to guarantee receiving a medal. **Wins → Receives a medal.** The rule doesn\'t tell us that winning is the only way to receive one.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep this:** The sufficient condition goes on the left. Meeting it is enough to guarantee the right.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 4. Necessary means required\\r\\n\\r\\nNow look at the other side:\\r\\n\\r\\n**Dog → Mammal**\\r\\n\\r\\nBeing a mammal is **necessary** for being a dog. A dog has to be a mammal.\\r\\n\\r\\nNecessary means required. It doesn\'t mean enough.\\r\\n\\r\\nReturn to the assignment:\\r\\n\\r\\n**Earns full credit → Passes**\\r\\n\\r\\nUnder this rule, passing is necessary for earning full credit. You can\'t earn full credit and fail. But knowing someone passed doesn\'t tell you they earned full credit.\\r\\n\\r\\nHere\'s a different example:\\r\\n\\r\\n> Entering the archive requires a pass.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Enters the archive → Has a pass**\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pass is required. That\'s why it goes on the right. Having a pass doesn\'t, by itself, establish that someone enters the archive.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Put the two sides together\\r\\n\\r\\n| Sufficient | Necessary |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| Enough to guarantee the other condition. | Required whenever the sufficient condition is met. |\\r\\n| Goes on the left. | Goes on the right. |\\r\\n| If I have this, what must follow? | What must I have in order for the left side to be true? |\\r\\n\\r\\nThese are two roles in the same relationship. You don\'t decide that a condition is always sufficient or always necessary. You read the particular rule.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Your turn\\r\\n\\r\\n> Every finalist receives an invitation.\\r\\n\\r\\nIdentify the sufficient condition and the necessary condition. Does receiving an invitation establish that someone is a finalist?\\r\\n\\r\\n<details>\\r\\n<summary>See the reasoning</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\nBeing a finalist is sufficient. Receiving an invitation is necessary. **Finalist → Receives an invitation.** Receiving one doesn\'t establish finalist status; the rule permits other people to receive invitations too.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep this:** Sufficient is enough. Necessary is required. Required means right.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 5. Group 1: Find the sufficient idea\\r\\n\\r\\nYou already understand the relationship. Now we\'re going to recognize the different ways a sentence can express it.\\r\\n\\r\\nOur Group 1 indicators are:\\r\\n\\r\\n**if · when · where · all · the only · every · any**\\r\\n\\r\\nThese introduce the sufficient idea. That complete idea goes on the left of the arrow.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe important question is: **“What is the indicator referring to?”**\\r\\n\\r\\n### Start with “if”\\r\\n\\r\\n> If a student revises the essay, the student receives feedback.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf what? If the student revises the essay.\\r\\n\\r\\nThat\'s the sufficient idea:\\r\\n\\r\\n**Revises the essay → Receives feedback**\\r\\n\\r\\nNow move the same clause:\\r\\n\\r\\n> A student receives feedback if the student revises the essay.\\r\\n\\r\\nIf what? Still, if the student revises the essay. The arrow stays the same. Sentence order changed; the relationship didn\'t.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The same relationship in other words\\r\\n\\r\\n| Sentence | What the indicator refers to | Translation |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| Every volunteer wears a badge. | Every volunteer. | Volunteer → Wears a badge |\\r\\n| Any applicant who submits late pays a fee. | Any applicant who submits late. | Applicant submits late → Pays a fee |\\r\\n| When the alarm sounds, the staff evacuate. | When the alarm sounds. | Alarm sounds → Staff evacuate |\\r\\n| Where there is smoke, there is fire. | Where there is smoke. | Smoke → Fire |\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep the complete idea. In the applicant sentence, “applicant” alone isn\'t enough. The rule applies to an applicant **who submits late**.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Read “the only” carefully\\r\\n\\r\\n> The only people admitted are members.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe only what? The only people admitted.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Admitted → Member**\\r\\n\\r\\nEveryone admitted must be a member. It doesn\'t tell us that every member is admitted.\\r\\n\\r\\nDon\'t skip “the.” We\'ll compare “the only” with “only” in the next lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Your turn\\r\\n\\r\\nFor each sentence, identify the indicator, ask what it refers to, and write the complete rule.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. All registered guests receive a wristband.\\r\\n2. A report is reviewed if it is submitted before noon.\\r\\n3. The only vehicles permitted inside are electric vehicles.\\r\\n\\r\\n<details>\\r\\n<summary>See the reasoning</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **All** refers to registered guests. Registered guest → Receives a wristband.\\r\\n2. **If** refers to submission before noon. Submitted before noon → Reviewed.\\r\\n3. **The only** refers to vehicles permitted inside. Vehicle permitted inside → Electric vehicle.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep this:** Find the indicator\'s target. For Group 1, that complete idea goes left.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 6. Group 2: Find what\'s required\\r\\n\\r\\nGroup 2 introduces the necessary idea. That complete idea goes on the right.\\r\\n\\r\\nOur Group 2 indicators are:\\r\\n\\r\\n**only · only if · only when · only where · always · requires · must**\\r\\n\\r\\nUse the same question: **“What is the indicator referring to?”**\\r\\n\\r\\n### Start with “only if”\\r\\n\\r\\n> A student enters the archive only if the student has a pass.\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly if what? Only if the student has a pass.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe pass is required:\\r\\n\\r\\n**Enters the archive → Has a pass**\\r\\n\\r\\nCompare that with “if”:\\r\\n\\r\\n| Sentence | Rule |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| A student enters if the student has a pass. | Has a pass → Enters |\\r\\n| A student enters only if the student has a pass. | Enters → Has a pass |\\r\\n\\r\\nThe first makes a pass enough. The second makes a pass required. One word changes what the sentence guarantees.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Required things can appear first\\r\\n\\r\\n> A pass is required for entry.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhat is required? A pass.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Enters → Has a pass**\\r\\n\\r\\nThe necessary idea appears before “required.” That\'s why we ask what the indicator refers to instead of automatically taking the words after it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Compare “only” and “the only”\\r\\n\\r\\n> Only members are admitted.\\r\\n\\r\\nOnly what? Only members. Being a member is required for admission.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Admitted → Member**\\r\\n\\r\\n> The only people admitted are members.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe only what? The only people admitted. That is the sufficient idea.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Admitted → Member**\\r\\n\\r\\nThese two sentences express the same rule. The indicator points to a different part of each sentence. Read the whole statement before deciding where each idea belongs.\\r\\n\\r\\n### More ways to state a requirement\\r\\n\\r\\n| Sentence | Required idea | Translation |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| A finalist must attend the interview. | Attends the interview. | Finalist → Attends interview |\\r\\n| Approval requires a signature. | Has a signature. | Approved → Has signature |\\r\\n| A review occurs only when a complaint is filed. | A complaint is filed. | Review occurs → Complaint filed |\\r\\n| The service operates only where a station is available. | A station is available. | Service operates → Station available |\\r\\n| A finalist always receives an invitation. | Receives an invitation. | Finalist → Receives invitation |\\r\\n\\r\\nHere, “always” expresses a rule without exceptions. Read it in context; a word by itself doesn\'t give you the complete relationship.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Your turn\\r\\n\\r\\nIdentify what\'s required, then write each rule.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Only registered guests receive wristbands.\\r\\n2. A permit is required for construction.\\r\\n3. A student graduates only if the student completes the project.\\r\\n\\r\\n<details>\\r\\n<summary>See the reasoning</summary>\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Registration is required. Receives wristband → Registered guest.\\r\\n2. A permit is required. Construction → Has permit.\\r\\n3. Completing the project is required. Graduates → Completes project.\\r\\n\\r\\n</details>\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep this:** For Group 2, the required idea goes right. Ask what the indicator refers to, then check the meaning of your arrow against the sentence.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## For our review: How the teaching and practice fit together\\r\\n\\r\\nThis section is editorial planning, not student-facing copy. Each lesson ends with its own drill before the student continues. Joshua can assign a whole chapter or an individual lesson and its practice. Students see their assigned work and its next step.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Lesson | Visual or guided interaction | Attached drill | What it establishes |\\r\\n|---|---|---|---|\\r\\n| 1. Guarantee | Reuse the nested-box activity shown in the supplied screenshot if its existing implementation correctly validates containment. Place dogs inside mammals; then place Luna inside dogs. No strict size claim: sets may be equal. | Distinguish guaranteed rules from “usually” claims; apply one explicit rule to a matching fact. | Student understands a guarantee and rule versus fact. |\\r\\n| 2. Direction | Place a cat inside mammals but outside dogs. Compare what the two starting facts allow. | Rule + fact: choose follows or undetermined, then explain. | Student applies the rule without reversing it. |\\r\\n| 3. Sufficient | Reveal “passes” when “earns full credit” is selected. Tighter is wasteful; significantly looser may cross the SIDTS server-\\r\\n  side validity window for your account/region.\\r\\n\\r\\n  Transient errors (e.g. ``httpx.RequestError`` from a flaky network) are\\r\\n  surfaced as exit 1 rather than retried in-process; the OS scheduler\'s next\\r\\n  firing is the retry mechanism.\\r\\n\\r\\n  With ``--verify``, after the refresh completes a read-only passive token\\r\\n  fetch confirms the resulting cookies actually authenticate, exiting non-zero\\r\\n  if not. While the provided sources do not detail every single LSAT Logical Reasoning question type (such as Parallel Reasoning or Method of Reasoning) they offer a comprehensive breakdown of the core activities required for analysis and specifically target the most critical error tested in Flaw questions. The breakdown of conditional logic primarily revolves around two main analytical activities: Chaining (deriving new rules) and Triggering (deriving new facts). I. General Breakdown Activity: Chaining Conditionals (Deriving New Rules). Chaining involves synthesizing multiple conditional rules to create a new inferred conditional statement. This is crucial for questions that require you to draw broad conclusions from a set of premises (often seen in Inference/Must Be True contexts). Connecting Rules: You must determine if the necessary condition (right side) of one conditional statement matches the sufficient condition (left side) of another. For instance if A rightarrow B and B rightarrow C they chain to infer a new conditional relationship: A rightarrow C. Contraposing Chains: You can contraposit an entire chain starting from the final necessary condition and negating back to the initial sufficient condition. If the chain is A rightarrow D the contrapositive is If not D then not A. The LSAT commonly rewards the ability to connect the beginning of the chain to the ending of the chain. Negating Complex Ideas: If the idea being contraposed (the trigger or the outcome) is a complex idea connected by and or or (e.g. A and B) you must remember to flip the truth values when negating. And turns into or and or turns into and. This ensures you correctly flip the truth value of everything in the complex idea. II. General Breakdown Activity: Triggering Conditionals (Deriving New Facts). Triggering is the process of using a known fact to activate a conditional rule and derive a certain factual inference. This is the process utilized in many Must Be True and Inference questions. A conditional rule (Sufficient rightarrow Necessary) can only be used in two valid scenarios: 1. Focus on finding Conditional Indicator words and using them as a way to organize how you write or think about the If-Then rule. Write or think through the contrapositive as well. Beware illegal Reversals or Negations. Conditional Logic by type Recap: Principle (the left side of the principle matches the evidence, the right side matches the conclusion). Parallel (diagramming these arguments with algebraic recipes allows us to be more picky and decisive when evaluating answers). Assumption (the conclusion gives us an A to Z logic path we want to prove, and the evidence + the correct answer choice assemble together to create that A to Z path). Must Be True / Most Supported (multiple conditionals often chain together, and provided facts often match the contrapositive-trigger of a conditional and allow us to infer the contrapositive-outcome). Flaw / Parallel Flaw (flaw + conditional logic usually means the necessary vs sufficient flaw using a rule in an illegal backwards or opposite fashion). instructions: Try these 10 questions in 22.5 minutes. Try to answer them all within your time limit, then circle back and confirm your thinking (untimed) before confirming your answers and reading the explanations, if available. CONDITIONAL KEYWORDS: Put on Left (sufficient conditions): if, when, any, each, all, every, the only, whenever, whoever. Put on Right (necessary conditions): only if, must, requires, ensures, always, implies, presupposes, depends on, guarantees. If-Not (negated version on left): unless, without, until, except. Negative to Positive conversions: No A are B = All A are not B. Not all A are B = Some A are not B. Few A are B = Most A are not B. Additional notes.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Source: intuition technique when stuck( conditional logic) .pdf\\r\\n\\r\\n**Path:** LSAT DUMP/LR/Conditional/Notes/intuition technique when stuck( conditional logic) .pdf  **Modified:** 2024-05-16T01:17:45+00:00  **Words:** 370  **Doc ID:** None\\r\\n\\r\\nHow to Figure Out Which Is Which: The What Test vs. Personalized If/Then The What Test The What Test is designed to resolve ambiguities in sentences with conditional indicators by pinpointing exactly what the indicator refers to. How to Perform the What Test This test involves adding a \\"what\\" to whichever side of the indicator makes grammatical sense, helping clarify the target of the condition. If what? People who what? Depends on what? When what? Each what? Need what? Any what? Must what? Have\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Source: intuition technique when stuck( conditional logic) .gdoc\\r\\n\\r\\n**Path:** LSAT DUMP/LR/Conditional/Notes/intuition technique when stuck( conditional logic) .gdoc  **Modified:** 2025-06-23T03:31:37.970000+00:00  **Words:** 370  **Doc ID:** 1ZthkbR3x5oHk9Rqv2ZOzR6j_tZ4HDsM45S_K0hBZlpA\\r\\n\\r\\nHow to Figure Out Which Is Which The What Test vs. Personalized If/Then. The What Test. The What Test is designed to resolve ambiguities in sentences with conditional indicators by pinpointing exactly what the indicator refers to. How to Perform the What Test. This test involves adding a what to whichever side of the indicator makes grammatical sense helping clarify the target of the condition. If what? People who what? Depends on what? When what? Each what? Need what? Any what? Must what? Have to what? All what? Whats necessary? Whats essential? Every what? Whats required? Whats the precondition? In order to what? Only (if) what? This test is typically unnecessary for straightforward indicators like if and all but proves invaluable for more confusing indicators such as depends and required. Example of The What Test. Sentence: Air is required for breathing. Implementation: Question: What is required in this sentence? Answer: Air is the thing that is required. Personalized If/Then Strategy. Personalized If/Then is a technique used to translate conditional statements into personal contexts simplifying understanding and ensuring correct logical diagramming. How to Create a Personalized If/Then. 1. Understand the casual non-conditional meaning of the sentence. 2. Take a guess at which half of the statement is the sufficient condition. 3. Put yourself in the situation of your guess and ask what you know about yourself. 4. If your guess is correct you will find that the necessary condition has to pertain. Example Translation into Personalized If/Then. Original Statement: Orchids depend on frequent conversation. Casual Meaning: Orchids need frequent conversation. Guess: Orchids as the sufficient condition. Personalization: If Im an orchid what do I know about me? I depend on frequent conversation. If Im an orchid then I have frequent conversation. This method not only aids in understanding the conditional but also verifies its correctness. Incorrect guesses can be easily identified and corrected through this personal context. Advantages of Personalized If/Then. Helps intuitively understand conditionals by imagining yourself as part of the scenario. Provides confidence throughout tests especially in correctly interpreting conditionals not phrased as if/then statements. Both the What Test and Personalized If/Then Strategy are crucial tools in deciphering and applying conditional logic particularly in competitive exams like the LSAT.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Source: Conditional Chains.pdf\\r\\n\\r\\n**Path:** LSAT DUMP/LR/Conditional/Notes/Conditional Chains.pdf  **Modified:** 2024-07-02T20:46:11+00:00  **Words:** 352  **Doc ID:** None\\r\\n\\r\\nConditional Chains Conditional statements are like Legos. They are more interesting when combined. You can latch them together in predictable ways. Example Statement 1: If I buy an espresso machine, I will end up in the highly-caffeinated poor house. Statement 2: If I end up in the highly-caffeinated poor house, I will finally be cool enough to wear non-ironic plaid. Let’s think each of these statements through. Let’s place ourselves in this situation and see what we know. Say I go ahead and mak\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Source: conditional worksheet.gdoc\\r\\n"}'}]

No hype, no em dashes, no invented LSAT statistics, no AI phrases such as unlock, delve or game-changer. Do not introduce contrapositives, Groups 3/4, chains or quantities. Sufficient means enough; necessary means required. Arrows express a relationship, not necessarily a cause or time order. A rule does not prove that its sufficient condition occurs. All dogs are mammals permits mammals that are not dogs and also does not require sets to have different sizes. Never automatically assign words after an indicator: ask what complete idea it refers to and check the whole meaning. Current Group 1 list: if, when, where, all, the only, every, any. Current Group 2 list: only, only if, only when, only where, always, requires, must. These are teaching groups, not universally mechanical word rules. Teach before testing.'''\n+VIDEO_PARTS = [\n+    ('01-what-conditionals-are', 'Teach what a conditional means using All dogs are mammals, Luna is a dog, therefore Luna is a mammal. download completed assets without clobbering.\"\"\"\n+import hashlib\n+import json\n+import pathlib\n+import subprocess\n+\n+ROOT = pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent\n+CLI = 'C:/Users/Joshu/.local/bin/notebooklm.exe'\n+manifest_path = ROOT / 'manifest.json'\n+manifest = json.loads(manifest_path.read_text(encoding='utf-8-sig'))\n+notebook = manifest['notebook_id']\n+result = subprocess.run([CLI, 'artifact', 'list', '-n', notebook, '--json'], capture_output=True, text=True, encoding='utf-8')\n+result.check_returncode()\n+by_id = {a['id']: a for a in json.loads(result.stdout)['artifacts']}\n+for asset in manifest['assets']:\n+    artifact_id = asset.get('generation', {}).get('task_id')\n+    live = by_id.get(artifact_id)\n+    if not live:\n+        continue\n+    asset['status'] = live['status']\n+    asset['generated_title'] = live['title']\n+    if live['status'] != 'completed':\n+        continue\n+    extension = {'report': 'md', 'flashcards': 'json', 'quiz': 'json', 'infographic': 'png', 'video': 'mp4'}[asset['type']]\n+    path = ROOT / (asset['slug'] + '.' + extension)\n+    if not path.exists():\n+        download = subprocess.run([CLI, 'download', asset['type'], str(path), '-n', notebook, '-a', artifact_id, '--no-clobber', '--json'], capture_output=True, text=True, encoding='utf-8')\n+        if download.returncode:\n+            asset['download_error'] = download.stderr or download.stdout\n+            continue\n+    asset['path'] = str(path)\n+    asset['sha256'] = hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()\n+    asset['bytes'] = path.stat().st_size\n+    asset['review_status'] = asset.get('review_status', 'Downloaded, not yet reviewed')\n+    print(json.dumps({'slug': asset['slug'], 'path': str(path), 'bytes': asset['bytes']}), flush=True)\n+manifest_path.write_text(json.dumps(manifest, indent=2), encoding='utf-8')\n+print(json.dumps({a['slug']: a['status'] for a in manifest['assets']}), flush=True)\n*** End Patch"));

text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch\n*** Add File: C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/notebooklm-opening-assets/REVIEW.md\n+# NotebookLM opening assets: review record\n+\n+Generated 2026-10-02 in notebook `e38c0aff-bb6e-498e-a5ef-a6b1bc3a6f5c`.\n+\n+Source: sanitized student teaching draft `teaching-source.md`, source ID `5f49c31e-848d-4eed-8cba-47f18e9636be`. No student transcripts, names, emails or private homework correspondence were uploaded. Generic fictional example names in the teaching draft are retained.\n+\n+Every generation uses only that explicit source. Prompts restrict content to what conditionals mean, why direction matters, sufficient, necessary, Group 1 and Group 2. `manifest.json` records artifact IDs, paths and SHA256 hashes. Downloaded files are original generation evidence. Files ending `-reviewed` are edited derivatives.\n+\n+## What was corrected\n+\n+- “A finalist must attend the interview” establishes an obligation, not actual compliance. Three flashcards, one quiz question and the report's table required correction.\n+- One flashcard incorrectly defined necessary as required whenever the outcome occurs. Corrected to required whenever the sufficient condition is met.\n+- One quiz accepted “submits late” despite asking for the complete applicant target. Removed that incomplete accepted answer.\n+- Feedback confused permission to enter with actual entry. Corrected.\n+- Two distractor rationales called different but compatible rules contradictions. Corrected to explain that those arrows do not express the original claim.\n+- The report overstated forward inference as the only valid conditional move. Corrected its scope and removed “Deep Dive” language.\n+- One flashcard introduced “whenever,” outside the current seven-word Group 1 list. Removed from this opening set.\n+\n+The reviewed files contain **79 flashcards and 27 quiz questions**, including multiple choice, multiple select, fill-in and short answer. This count does not certify an app renderer supports every type. Platform integration must map each type or deliberately adapt it.\n+\n+## Visual review\n+\n+The sufficient/necessary infographic was opened and inspected. Its nested-set relationship, direction comparison, Group 1/2 lists and only/the-only examples are accurate. It uses a cream background, ink serif headings and watercolor illustrations. It is a reference image rather than a replacement for interactive set manipulation. Small-screen legibility needs app verification.\n+\n+## Video release condition\n+\n+Six separate brief videos were submitted, one per opening part. Until each downloaded video is watched, its status is **not reviewed**. The source's original interview sentence may propagate the obligation/compliance error into Group 2. Do not publish or embed that video without checking it. Do not claim generated narration is Joshua's voice. Voice imitation was not requested or generated.\n+\n+Source correction should be incorporated into any subsequent generation. No existing notebook assets were deleted.\n*** End Patch"));

', teaching)[1:]\n+slugs = ['01-what-conditionals-are', '02-why-direction-matters', '03-sufficient-means-enough', '04-necessary-means-required', '05-group-one', '06-group-two']\n+path = ROOT / 'scoped-video-manifest.json'\n+manifest = json.loads(path.read_text()) if path.exists() else {'notebook_id': NOTEBOOK, 'date': '2026-10-02', 'assets': []}\n+for index, (slug, section) in enumerate(zip(slugs, sections)):\n+    asset = next((a for a in manifest['assets'] if a['slug'] == slug), None)\n+    if asset is None:\n+        asset = {'slug': slug, 'type': 'video', 'revision_reason': 'First video prompts expanded beyond individual lesson. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 2.4 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"66d71b","wall_time_seconds":2.2366091,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":572,"output":"{\\r\\n  \\"source_id\\": \\"f254f4bf-fd40-4a13-b474-123f07b86fc3\\",\\r\\n  \\"title\\": \\"01-what-conditionals-are.mp4\\",\\r\\n  \\"kind\\": \\"media\\",\\r\\n  \\"content\\": \\"Welcome to this explainer on LSAT conditional logic. We will focus on rules, not blind word memorization. We will cover what a rule provides, direction, sufficient and necessary conditions and two indicator groups. Section one, what a rule gives you. We have to start by understanding logical guarantees. Let\'s take a basic rule. All dogs are mammals. This guarantees a very specific relationship. A rule tells you what must be true. A fact like Luna being a dog applies it. Now put it perfectly inside a cobalt box of mammals. When we put Luna inside that dog, she has to be a mammal, too. Section two, rules have a direction. Let\'s explore why these rules flow one specific way. An arrow shows a relationship. It absolutely does not mean cause or time order. The rule allows mammals that are not dogs. So, we cannot just reverse the direction. Section three, sufficient and necessary. The crucial point is understanding both sides of this logical relationship. Sufficient simply means enough. Being a dog is enough to guarantee it is a mammal. Necessary means required. A dog is required to be a mammal. This required condition goes right. Section four, group one indicators. Let\'s see how specific words introduce these conditions. These group on words introduce the sufficient condition that goes on the left side. Never blindly assign words after an indicator. Always ask what complete idea it actually targets. Here the word every refers to volunteers. So volunteers go on the left side. Section five group two indicators. Let\'s see how we find the necessary condition instead. Group two words introduce the necessary idea. That required idea always goes on the right. Ask what the require idea is do not just apply a mechanical word rule. Let\'s compare two similar sentences to see how the logic operates in real life. Both mean admission requires being a member. They share the exact same directional relationship. You have to read the whole statement before deciding where each complete idea belongs. Always ask if the rule gives you this exact result. Have you verified the complete meaning?\\\\n\\",\\r\\n  \\"url\\": null,\\r\\n  \\"char_count\\": 2102\\r\\n}\\r\\n"}'}]

'scoped-video-manifest.json'\n+manifest = json.loads(manifest_path.read_text())\n+def run(args):\n+    response = subprocess.run([CLI, *args], capture_output=True, text=True, encoding='utf-8')\n+ text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch\n*** Add File: C:/Users/Joshu/dev/ai-os/brainstorms/2026-09-30-conditional-curriculum/notebooklm-opening-assets/generate_original_order_videos.py\n+\"\"\"Original opening scenarios, replacing borrowed dog/mammal teaching examples.\"\"\"\n+import json\n+import subprocess\n+from pathlib import Path\n+\n+ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent\n+CLI = 'C:/Users/Joshu/.local/bin/notebooklm.exe'\n+NOTEBOOK = 'e38c0aff-bb6e-498e-a5ef-a6b1bc3a6f5c'\n+LESSONS = [\n+('01-what-conditionals-are', '''# What a conditional tells you\n+\n+Imagine a pickup counter. There is one rule: Every order marked ready has been packed.\n+\n+Order A is marked ready. What do you know about it? It has been packed. You do not need to open the bag to find that out. The rule covers every order marked ready, and Order A is one of those orders.\n+\n+That is a conditional. When one condition is met, another must be met too. Here, being marked ready gives you packed.\n+\n+Marked ready → Packed.\n+\n+Read it in English: If an order is marked ready, it has been packed. The arrow records the relationship. It does not tell us what caused either condition or which happened first.\n+\n+The rule and the fact do different jobs. The rule applies to every order marked ready. The fact tells us that Order A meets that condition. Together, they tell us something else about Order A.\n+\n+Show all ready orders inside a packed-orders boundary. The packed boundary can contain other orders too. The rule does not require the groups to differ in size. No ready order can sit outside packed.\n+\n+Pause: Order C is marked ready. Has it been packed? Yes. It meets the condition the rule covers.\n+\n+We have not claimed that every packed order is marked ready. That question comes next.\n+'''),\n+('02-why-direction-matters', '''# Why the direction matters\n+\n+Keep the same pickup-counter rule: Every order marked ready has been packed.\n+\n+Marked ready → Packed.\n+\n+Order A is marked ready. The rule tells us it has been packed.\n+\n+Now look at Order B. It has been packed. Is it marked ready? We cannot tell from this rule. Order B might already be marked ready. It might be packed while it waits for a pickup label. Both possibilities fit.\n+\n+Notice what changed. With Order A, we knew the condition the rule starts from. With Order B, we only knew the other side.\n+\n+The rule promises that ready orders are packed. It does not promise that all packed orders are ready. Before accepting a conclusion, check that the rule actually gives it to you.\n+\n+On the LSAT, this helps you see what follows in a Must Be True question. It also helps you spot an argument that reverses a rule and concludes more than its evidence supports. Later, the same relationships help connect evidence to a conclusion.\n+\n+Visual: ready orders fit inside packed orders. Put Order A inside ready. Put two possible versions of Order B in packed: one in ready, one outside ready. Neither violates the rule.\n+\n+Pause: Order D is packed. Does that prove it is not ready? No. Its ready status is undetermined. It could be ready or not ready.\n+'''),\n+('03-sufficient-means-enough', '''# Sufficient means enough\n+\n+Every order marked ready has been packed.\n+\n+Marked ready → Packed.\n+\n+Being marked ready is sufficient for having been packed. Sufficient means enough. Once we know the order is marked ready, we have what we need to conclude it has been packed.\n+\n+Take Order A. It is marked ready. Under the rule, can it be unpacked? No. That would break the rule.\n+\n+But being marked ready may not be the only way an order can be packed. Order B could be packed while it waits for its pickup label. The rule allows that.\n+\n+Enough does not mean the only way. That difference matters.\n+\n+The sufficient condition goes on the left. Do not choose it because it appears first in the sentence. Choose it because meeting that condition guarantees the other one.\n+\n+Visual: select the ready label on Order A and reveal its packed status. Then show a packed Order B whose ready status is unknown. Keep the arrow ready → packed.\n+\n+Pause: We know Order C is marked ready. What does the rule give us? It has been packed. Being marked ready is enough to establish that.\n+\n+We are describing a relationship, not claiming that a ready label causes an order to be packed.\n+'''),\n+('04-necessary-means-required', '''# Necessary means required\n+\n+Every order marked ready has been packed.\n+\n+Marked ready → Packed.\n+\n+Packed is necessary for being marked ready under this rule. A ready order has to be packed. You cannot have a ready order that is unpacked without breaking the rule.\n+\n+Necessary means required. Required does not mean enough.\n+\n+Order B has been packed. That gives it something every ready order has. But it does not establish that Order B is marked ready. It might still be waiting for a pickup label.\n+\n+Compare the two roles in the same rule. Being marked ready is enough to establish packed. Being packed is required whenever an order is marked ready.\n+\n+Marked ready is sufficient, on the left. Packed is necessary, on the right. Required means right.\n+\n+These are roles in this relationship. A condition is not always sufficient or always necessary in every rule.
